# Deubiquitinase Processing of a Non-Natural Linkage of Ubiquitinated-PTEN

**Authors:** Reina Iwase; Isabella Jaen Maisonet; Kwangwoon Lee; Sara J. Buhrlage; Philip A. Cole

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Blavatnik Institute, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts 02115, United States | bDivision of Genetics, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts 02115, United States | cDepartment of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, United States

## Abstract

PTEN is an important tumor suppressor protein that is regulated by ubiquitination events which are modulated by deubiquitinases, or enzymes that remove ubiquitin from substrate proteins. As ubiquitinated substrates are beneficial to study deubiquitinase activity and substrate recognition, we have previously developed a semisynthetic strategy to site-specifically install a monoubiquitin on PTEN. This strategy uses a non-natural aminoAla-Cys functionality as a convenient alternative to the synthetically more challenging natural isopeptide linkage. However, the effective processing of this linkage by deubiquitinases other than by the deubiquitinase USP7 has not been evaluated.

Therefore, we assessed whether the aminoAla-Cys linked monoubiquitinated PTEN can be processed by other known deubiquitinases. We found that USP10, USP11, and USP15 processed monoubiquitinated PTEN but BAP1 and OTUD3 could not under the conditions tested. This study demonstrates that ubiquitin linked to the aminoAla-Cys functionality is hydrolyzable by members of the USP family deubiquitinases and enables the systematic evaluation of deubiquitinase activities toward monoubiquitinated protein substrates.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Phosphatase and human homolog (PTEN) is a tumor suppressor protein in the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway and acts as a lipid phosphatase to dephosphorylate membrane localized PI(3,4,5)P3 to PI(4,5)P2, preventing downstream Akt activation and signaling for cell survival and proliferation [1,2]. PTEN’s stability, activity, and localization are regulated by ubiquitination events. PTEN can be polyubiquitinated and be subject to proteasomal-dependent degradation [3–5] or prevented from being recruited to the plasma membrane [6,7]. In addition, PTEN can be monoubiquitinated and undergo nuclear translocation [8–10], where it performs nuclear functions regulating DNA repair, chromosome stability, cell cycle progression, and transcription [11–13].

Multiple deubiquitinases, enzymes that hydrolyze the amide bond between the ubiquitin C-terminal carboxyl and the Lys sidechain amino group, appear to influence the level of PTEN ubiquitination [14,15] (Fig. 1). BAP1 [16], OTUD3 [17], USP11 [18], and USP13 [19] have each been reported to serve as PTEN deubiquitinases that stabilize PTEN protein levels by decreasing polyubiquitination. Other deubiquitinases such as USP7 [20] and USP10 [19,21] are proposed to affect cellular localization of PTEN [16,17]. These deubiquitinases are classified into different families with unique catalytic domain folds and a range of substrate specificities [22–24]. USP7, USP10, USP11 and USP13 belong to the ubiquitin-specific protease (USP) family, which is the largest family of deubiquitinases [25,26]. USPs generally have one strong ubiquitin binding site and do not have a strong secondary ubiquitin binding site [22,25]. OTUD3 belongs to the ovarian tumor protease (OTU) family which are generally considered to be more substrate selective than the USPs, as the OTU family members have additional ubiquitin binding sites in the catalytic domain that confer specificity for ubiquitin chains [27,28]. Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase (UCH) family members, including BAP1, have a crossover loop that appears to restrict the size of the substrates they can deubiquitinate [29].

Protein semisynthesis has been widely used to prepare site-specifically modified proteins to decipher the roles of the specific modification for the protein of interest [30,31]. However, generating ubiquitinated proteins with natural isopeptide bonds is synthetically challenging. The available methods require complex multi-step synthesis of ligation auxiliaries or thiolated lysine building blocks [32–35], limiting the scope of use. Therefore, approaches to install ubiquitin on target proteins with non-natural isopeptide linkages are valuable alternatives for studying the regulation of proteins by ubiquitination [36,37]. Several approaches to incorporating ubiquitin through non-standard linkages have been developed including acetonyl-thioethers [38,39], disulfides [40–42], and triazoles [43,44] (Fig. 2). While useful in a number of applications, these approaches are typically not amenable to enzymatic turnover by deubiquitinases, limiting their utility in investigating deubiquitinase action. Other approaches such as thiol-ene coupling [45], installation of hydrazide mimics [46], or cysteine-aminoethylation-assisted chemical ubiquitination [47] result in ubiquitinated proteins that can be processed by deubiquitinases, but milder reaction conditions may be necessary for some complex protein substrates.

We have therefore recently developed a semisynthetic strategy to install ubiquitin on tumor suppressor PTEN protein via a novel non-natural ubiquitin linkage with an aminoalanine-cysteine (aminoAla-Cys) functionality [48]. The aminoAla-Cys linkage has a similar atomic spacing of a native Lys-ubiquitin but possesses an amide in the sidechain and includes a thiomethyl group appended near the epsilon amino group position (Fig 3A). Sequential expressed protein ligations of PTEN segments and recombinant ubiquitin protein were performed to obtain a PTEN (aa1-16) ubiquitin-peptide conjugate and near full-length PTEN protein (aa1-378) that were monoubiquitinated at aa13 position (Fig 3B). Our prior work has demonstrated that PTEN (aa1-16) ubiquitin-peptide conjugate with various linkages showed similar deubiquitination rates as the natural Lys-Ub PTEN peptide for processing by the deubiquitinase USP7 [48]. This finding suggests that substrates with non-natural linked ubiquitin may be used for deubiquitinase assays. However, the ability for other known deubiquitinases of PTEN to process the aminoAla-Cys functionality has not been evaluated. We have therefore assessed whether the aminoAla-Cys containing ubiquitinated PTEN peptide conjugate and PTEN protein can be processed by USP10, USP11, USP13, OTUD3, and BAP1 which are known deubiquitinases of PTEN.

## Results and Discussion

### Expression of recombinant deubiquitinase

To examine whether the Ub-aminoAla-Cys linkage can be processed by various deubiquitinases, we expressed and purified a panel of deubiquitinases (USP10, USP11, USP13, OTUD3, and BAP1) which are suggested to regulate PTEN protein. Additionally, we prepared a highly active and promiscuous USP15 deubiquitinase [26] that has no identified function in PTEN regulation. All constructs were expressed in E. coli and produced sufficient amounts of enzyme for assays, but with variable purities (Fig. 4A). The activity of the purified deubiquitinases were tested using a ubiquitin-Rhodamine110 (Ub-Rho110) tool reagent [49]. Ub-Rho110 can be generated by a ligation of ubiquitin(aa1-75)-MESNa thioester with bis-glycyl-Rhodamine110 [49,50], and this tool is commonly used for deubiquitinase screening [51,52]. All deubiquitinase constructs except for full-length USP10 and USP13 had measurable activity in processing Ub-Rho110 (Fig. 4B, 4C). The lack of catalytic activity of recombinant USP10 and USP13 with Ub-Rho110 produced in this way is consistent with prior reports [53,54]. In any event, we proceeded with testing the full panel of recombinant deubiquitinases for their ability to process PTEN substrates with non-natural ubiquitin linkages.

### Deubiquitination of PTEN substrates with aminoAla-Cys functionality

The purified deubiquitinases were tested for their ability to hydrolyze ubiquitin from monoubiquitinated substrates of PTEN (aa1-16) peptide and PTEN (aa1-378) linked through aminoAla-Cys. As mentioned, the aminoAla-Cys linkage was developed as a surrogate for ubiquitinated substrates that can be more easily prepared. Liquid chromatography and electrospray mass spectrometric analysis of the ubiquitinated samples revealed successful formation of ubiquitinated PTEN peptide and ubiquitinated PTEN protein products (Fig 5). Among the deubiquitinases that were active against Ub-Rho110, the deubiquitinases USP7, USP10 catalytic domain (USP10CD), USP11, and USP15 were able to deubiquitinate both the peptide and protein forms of ubiquitinated PTEN (Fig 6 and Fig 7). Although USP15 serving as a PTEN deubiquitinase has not been reported previously, USP15’s activity is not very surprising considering its promiscuity [26]. BAP1 showed weak activity against ubiquitinated-peptide and no detectable activity against ubiquitinated PTEN protein despite the high activity against Ub-Rho110 substrate. The weak BAP1 activity can be rationalized by the large substrate size of ubiquitinated PTEN. UCH deubiquitinases like BAP1 appear to have restricted space for substrate binding due to the presence of a conserved crossover loop [29]. OTUD3 had no detectable activity with both PTEN substrates tested, consistent with OTUD3’s weak activity against monoubiquitinated substrates [17], as OTUD3 is known to primarily hydrolyze ubiquitin chains [27]. These results suggest that the aminoAla-Cys linkage can be generally processed by members of the USP family, but further studies will ultimately be needed to verify the generalizability of this linkage to other deubiquitinase families.

## Conclusion

The use of non-natural linkages reduces the barrier to prepare site-specifically ubiquitinated proteins for biochemical studies. Enzymatic processing of Ub-aminoAla-Cys was evaluated using a panel of known PTEN deubiquitinases. Substrates with the Ub-aminoAla-Cys linkage contain a reactive sulfhydryl group that can potentially interfere with the deubiquitination reaction. However, we expect the sulfhydryl to be tolerated based on our previous study where we showed comparable deubiquitination rates by USP7 between the aminoAla-Cys linkage and the corresponding desulfurized analog (amioAla-Ala).[48] Among the deubiquitinases that we were able to prepare in active forms, we were able to show that USP10CD, USP11, and USP15 can deubiquitinate the Ub-aminoAla-Cys peptide conjugate in addition to USP7. Monoubiquitinated PTEN could not be processed by BAP1 or OTUD3 under the conditions tested. This may be due to a defect on the part of the deubiquitinase due to the limitations of bacterial expression, such as the lack of interacting proteins or modifications that might activate the deubiquitinase. For example, BAP1 may require complex formation with other interacting proteins such as ASXL1, for activity towards large substrates [55,56]. Alternatively, the lack of activity could be due to an unsuitable substrate because OTUD3 primarily hydrolyzes ubiquitinated chains [27] and BAP1 has restricted space in the active site [29]. Given the challenges of producing large quantities of Ub-PTEN, it was not feasible to measure the binding affinities of Ub-PTEN with the various DUBs. However, the functional insights into the various processing events of Ub-PTEN by DUBs provide valuable biochemical insights into these enzyme-substrate interactions.

Our current study is also limited to the preparation of monoubiquitinated substrates, but the deubiquitinases tested (USP10, USP11, USP13, OTUD3, and BAP1) are known regulators of polyubiquitinated PTEN. Therefore, preparation of ubiquitinated PTEN with variable ubiquitin chains in the future will be needed to evaluate the more physiological behavior of these deubiquitinases. Despite these limitations, we have demonstrated that the ubiquitin from the aminoAla-Cys linkage is hydrolyzable by USP family deubiquitinases and indicate the utility of this approach in studies on molecular recognition. We envision aminoAla-Cys linkage to be used to prepare complex ubiquitinated substrates for structural studies with catalytically deficient DUB mutants, to capture high resolution structures of the enzyme-substrate complexes.

## Materials and Methods

### DNA plasmids and proteins

DNA plasmid of USP15 (aa2-981) with an N-terminal 6xHis-MBP (maltose binding protein) fusion (KanR) was a kind gift from Dr. Champak Chatterjee (University of Washington). BAP1 protein (Catalog #E-345) was purchased from Boston Biochem and USP10CD (aa376-798) protein was produced by the DFCI Structure and Chemical Biology Core.

### Protein expression and purification

#### Expression and purification of USP7

USP7 (aa1-1102) was expressed and purified as described in Iwase et al [48]. In brief, USP7 in pET28aLIC plasmid was transformed into BL21 (DE3) cells and cultured in LB media at 37°C until OD600 = 0.6, and induced with 0.5 mM IPTG at 16°C overnight. The cells were harvested and USP7 was purified over a Ni-column, MonoQ column, and Superdex200 column.

#### Expression and purification of USP10 FL, USP11, USP13, USP15, OTUD3

Plasmids of USP10 (aa1-798) in pET28PP (KanR), USP11 (aa1-920) in pGEX4T1 (AmpR), and USP13 (aa1-863) in pET42c (KanR) were transformed into BL21 (DE3) cells, USP15 plasmid was transformed into LOBSTR Rosetta (DE3) cells and the OTUD3 (aa52-275) plasmid in pOPINK (KanR) was transformed into E.coli Rosetta (DE3) pLysS cells. The cells were cultured in LB media with the respective antibiotics (50 μg/mL kanamycin or 100 μg/mL ampicillin) at 37°C until OD600 = 0.6–0.8 was reached. Cultures for USP10, USP11, and USP15 were induced with 0.5 mM IPTG at 16–18°C and further grown overnight. The USP13 culture was induced with 10 μM IPTG at 16°C and further grown for 48 h. The OTUD3 culture was induced with 0.5 mM IPTG at 20°C and further grown overnight.

#### For USP11, USP13, OTUD3:

The cells were harvested, re-suspended in lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 1 mM PMSF, 1 tablet of Pierce protease inhibitor cocktail), and lysed by passing through a French press three times. The debris was pelleted by centrifuging the lysate at 27,000g for 40 min, and the lysate was loaded onto GSH-agarose resin (MCLAB, Catalog #GAB-300) pre-equilibrated with 25 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP. The lysate was flowed through slowly, and the resin was washed with 10 column volumes of wash buffer 1 (25 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 0.1% Triton X-100) and 10 column volumes of wash buffer 2 (25 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP). The GST-tagged deubiquitinases were eluted with 50 mM reduced glutathione in wash buffer 2. USP11 protein solution was dialyzed against MonoQ Buffer A (50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 20 mM NaCl, 10 mM DTT) overnight at 4°C, and purified using a MonoQ anion exchange column with a 180 mL gradient of 0–50% B (50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 10 mM DTT). The purified fractions containing USP11 were pooled and eluted over a Superdex 200 column with a mobile phase of 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 200 mM NaCl, 10 mM DTT. USP13 and OTUD3 were also purified over a Superdex 200 column. The purified fractions were pooled, concentrated with a buffer containing final 5% glycerol, flash frozen, and stored at −80°C until use.

#### For USP10:

The cells were harvested, re-suspended in lysis buffer (100 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 20 mM imidazole, 1 mM PMSF, 1 tablet of EDTA-free Pierce protease inhibitor cocktail), and lysed by passing through a french press three times. The debris was pelleted by centrifuging the lysate at 27,000g for 40 min, and the lysate was loaded on Ni-NTA resin pre-equilibrated with wash buffer 1 (100 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 20 mM imidazole). The column was then washed with 5 column volumes of wash buffer 1 and 5 column volumes of wash buffer 2 (100 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 60 mM imidazole) prior to elution with 2 column volumes of elution buffer (100 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 250 mM imidazole). The eluted fractions were pooled, concentrated, and dialyzed against 25 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP. The dialyzed proteins were purified over a Superdex 200 column with a mobile phase of 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 200 mM NaCl, 10 mM DTT, 5% glycerol. The purified fractions were pooled, concentrated, flash frozen, and stored at −80°C until use.

#### For USP15:

The cells were harvested, re-suspended in lysis buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.6, 200 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP) and lysed by passing through a french press three times. The debris was pelleted by centrifuging the lysate at 27,000g for 40 min, and the lysate was loaded on Ni-NTA resin pre-equilibrated with the lysis buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.6, 200 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP). The lysate was incubated with the resin, and the resin was washed with 10 column volumes of wash buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.6, 200 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 50 mM imidazole) prior to elution with elution buffer (20 mM Tris pH 7.6, 200 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 200 mM imidazole). 5 mM EDTA was added to the eluted protein, and the sample was buffer-exchanged against the lysis buffer using a 100 kDa MWCO Amicon concentrator. The purified protein was flash frozen and stored at −80°C until use.

### Protein semisynthesis

Ubiquitinated PTEN (aa1-16) peptide and ubiquitinated PTEN (aa1-378) protein were semisynthesized as described in Iwase et al [48]. In brief, ubiquitin (aa1-76) was expressed as an intein-chitin binding domain fusion from E.coli Rosetta (DE3) pLysS cells and purified as a C-terminal thioester through intein cleavage by MESNa. The ubiquitin-thioester was ligated to PTEN peptide (aa1-16) synthesized by solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) on a Wang resin. The ubiquitinated PTEN (aa1-16) peptide was purified through MonoS cation exchange column and Superdex75 column.

For the semisynthesis of ubiquitinated PTEN protein, ubiquitin-thioester was prepared with a N-terminal His8 tag and ligated to PTEN peptide (aa1-16) with a C-terminal o-aminoanilide moiety synthesized by SPPS on a Dawson Dbz NovaSynTGR resin (Novabiochem, Catalog #855142). The C-terminal o-aminoanilide moiety of the ubiquitinated PTEN (1–16) peptide was subsequently activated by NaNO2 for ligation with PTENQ17C (aa17-378) expressed and purified from High Five cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The ligated protein product was purified through the Superdex200 10/300 GL increase column and HisTrap FF column (Cytiva).

The purified proteins were characterized by LC-MS using a Vanquish Flex LC (ThermoFisher Scientific) interfaced to a Q Exactive mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific). Protein samples were passed over a MAbPac RP 3 μM 2.1 × 100mm column (ThermoFisher, catalog no. 088647) with a linear gradient of 5–80% mobile phase B at 0.3 ml/min in 5 min for Ub-PTEN peptide and 10 min for Ub-PTEN protein, where mobile phase A was water + 0.1% formic acid and B was acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid.

### Deubiquitinase assays

#### Ub-Rho110 Deubiquitinase Assay

Ub-Rho110 deubiquitinase assays were conducted in a 384-well black plate at a 30 μL scale with assay buffer (50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 5 mM TCEP, 1 mg/mL ovalbumin). Deubiquitinases and Ub-Rho110 were separately diluted to 2x concentrations with assay buffer. Upon mixing the deubiquitinases and Ub-Rho110, the fluorescence intensity was recorded at one-minute intervals up to 60 min using a Biotek Cytation 5 plate reader at 25°C (Ex: 485 nm, Em: 535 nm). The linear range of the fluorescence vs. time plots was used to calculate the initial rates.

#### SDS-PAGE gel-based deubiquitinase assay

Assays for ubiquitinated-peptide were performed at 25°C with 5 μM substrate in the presence of 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 5 mM DTT, and 0.05 mg/mL BSA. At the 10 min time point, 4 μL of sample was removed and quenched by the addition of 4 μL of 2x SDS-loading dye and boiling for 5 min. The no DUB control was taken by removing the reaction sample prior to deubiquitinase addition and adding back denatured deubiquitinase with SDS-loading dye and boiling. Each sample was run on a 17% Tris-Tricine gel or 4–12% Bolt Bis-Tris gel for visualization by staining with Colloidal Blue Staining Kit. The intensity of the product and substrate bands were quantified using Image J and the average rate of deubiquitination was calculated as follows: Substrate × Band Intensity of Product − Background Band Intensity of Product − Background + Band Intensity of Substrate × 1 Time

#### Western blot-based deubiquitinase assay

Assays for ubiquitinated PTEN protein were performed at the similar conditions as the ubiquitinated-peptide, except for the use of 500 nM substrate. At the 5 min time point, 2 μL of sample was removed and quenched by the addition of 2 μL of 2x SDS-loading dye and boiling for 5 min. The quenched samples were loaded on a 10% Tris-Glycine gel or 4–20% Tris-Glycine gel. For Western blotting, the gel was transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane using an iBlot semi-dry blotting system with the P3 (20 V) setting for 7 min (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The membrane was blocked with 5% BSA in TBST buffer for 1 h, incubated with anti-PTEN (D5G7) antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Catalog #5384, 1:1000 dilution) with 2% BSA in TBST at 4°C overnight. Upon incubation with HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Catalog #7074, 1:2000 dilution) for 1 h and TBST washes, the bands were visualized with Clarity Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad, Catalog #1705061). For data analysis, the intensities of the Western blot bands were quantified using ImageJ.
